name: Triplasiella
look_here_first: LOVEGRASS TRIDENS: look for an open, sparse, broadly spreading, often drooping panicle with many small separated spikelets. But other native Tridens and Eragrostis can ALSO be airy! Follow a real plant from crown to flower head, then under a lens verify a 3-veined lemma approx. 2–3.5 mm where ONLY the midnerve may project as a short point, and check the actual membranous ragged ligule. Without attached ruler-scaled spikelet and collar, label Triplasiella SUSPECTED rather than confirmed.

recognition.where_to_look_first: LOVEGRASS TRIDENS: a fine open, arching and widely spreading lovegrass-like panicle with tiny dispersed spikelets, unlike compact narrow Tridens heads. Confirmation requires a mature 3-veined lemma, glumes and ligule under magnification, not merely a large airy grass panicle. Historical synonym Tridens eragrostoides is NOT another canonical species.
priority: Species exact original photos (first two panels): see widely separated fine branches and separate reddish mature spikelets; ignore other bristly grass in Powell image background.
Purpletop and Texas tridens can ALSO have open arching flowering heads; crosscompare the source labelled other-species panels rather than rely on airy vs compact.
MATURE FLORET macro (not yet archived): observe 3 longitudinal lemma nerves, only a short central mucro, measure 2–3.5 mm mature lemma; Kew and Flora Neomexicana context.
TRUE LIGULE macro (not archived): open blade–sheath junction and inspect a short ragged membranous ligule with mm scale; source historical descriptions give approx. 1.2–3 mm.
GROWTH FORM photo (not archived): source botanical descriptions describe a tufted perennial with sometimes short knotty rhizomatous base; do not assume no rhizomes.
recognition.field_caution: Photo-similarity is a LOW-confidence ID. Do NOT declare T. eragrostoides from open panicle alone, or claim the close-up lemma/ligule is already photographed. Historical Tridens eragrostoides and Tridentopsis eragrostoides are synonyms, not extra learner species. Hays county source/provisional flag untouched.

comparison_lesson.title: Triplasiella eragrostoides vs 3 native photographed grass look-alikes
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: 2 TARGET real photos → 3 native other-species reference photos → find measured mature lemma and true ligule; don't call it from an airy head.
quick_split: TARGET Triplasiella eragrostoides — fairly broad open panicle, fine distant branches, darkening small spikelets; prior name Tridens eragrostoides. A midnerve that alone extends as a short projection is a useful fine distinction in Flora Neomexicana.
NATIVE purpletop Tridens flavus — spreading/drooping OPEN panicle too, often purplish; beware previous overgeneralization that all Tridens are contracted.
NATIVE Texas tridens Tridens texanus — arching open panicle, potentially quite similar from several feet away. Measure/inspect mature spikelet and lemma instead of using panicle outline as sole key.
NATIVE purple lovegrass Eragrostis spectabilis — airy colored panicle and tuft, often superficially similar; check florets/lemma architecture in a confirmed plant.

Triplasiella vs sandgrass Triplasis: the 2016 taxonomic treatment reports MUCH broader target panicles and different palea keels, plus absence of upper-sheath cleistogamous spikelets; those features are not verified in current images.
comparison_lesson.guardrail: Triplasiella remains one canonical species in the project. No taxonomy/range reevaluation or native county scores in this pass.

what_to_teach_crew: Start on TWO real source-labelled photos for Triplasiella; the second has a bristly seedhead of an unrelated grass in the right background. Never arrow it as the target.
Purpletop and Texas tridens are native and ALSO have open panicles. Do not teach the erroneous 'all Tridens have contracted heads' shortcut.
Inspect mature lemma under 10–20x: 3 veins, one short protruding middle tip; historical descriptions give 2–3.5 mm. The current photographs are NOT magnified enough to demonstrate this.
Open the blade–sheath junction and examine the inner lacerate membranous ligule with ruler; do not confuse with hairy blade edges. No confirmed ligule pixels in current gallery.
Confirm full plant architecture and attached flowering structure on same source-verified individual; hand photo provides crude context but not a calibrated scale.
Do not create another card called Tridens eragrostoides — it is the previous name of Triplasiella eragrostoides.
Maintain the existing Hays county PROVISIONAL status; general Texas nativity is not a complete Hays voucher audit.
visual_needs: HIGHEST—mature T. eragrostoides actual ruler-calibrated lemma photo, unambiguously three dorsal nerves and single projecting midnerve; historical Fig. 97(d), Scribner 1900 (public domain), has exact-species line illustration but is not a newly installed photo.
SECOND: true 1–3 mm ragged MEMBRANOUS ligule revealed at actual blade/sheath inner surface with a 1-mm ruler and precise arrow.
THIRD: intact rooted T. eragrostoides perennial with full attached mature panicle and short rhizomatous/knotty base visible without damaging uncommon native population.
FOURTH: matched macro comparison with native Tridens flavus and T. texanus mature lemma apex, not just whole flowerheads.
FIFTH: verify original photo-2 species voucher/GBIF photo-level license and ensure unrelated background grass is not mistaken for target.

primary.original_title: American grasses — F. Lamson-Scribner, Washington Government Printing Office, 1900
primary.description: Printed page 128, Figure 97. Source caption lists (a) spikelet, (b) glumes-separated spikelet, (c) florets, (d) dorsal view of the flowering glume (= lemma), and (e) palea.
primary.copyright: PUBLIC DOMAIN — Smithsonian Libraries and Archives / Biodiversity Heritage Library verifies 1900 original public domain
primary.relevance: Exact original historical species figured, mature lemma dorsal view identified as Fig. 97(d), specifically useful anatomy guide, not a photo, not millimeter-calibrated

secondary.work: George Vasey, Grasses of the Southwest, vol. II, 1891, plate 34: Triodia eragrostoides
secondary.note: Two catalog entries identify exact old-name plate t.34; original illustrated plate can be reviewed as species-level identification reference; not yet cropped or inspected for individual lemma vein evidence.

modern_species_diagnosis.quote_less_paraphrase: In key for historical Tridens eragrostoides, lemmas ca. 2–3 mm with only midnerve extended as a short point vs larger purpletop and mid+side nerves projecting.
modern_species_diagnosis.taxonomic_guard: Accepted genus Triplasiella from 2016; original synonyms Triodia/Tridens/Tridentopsis NOT independent species.
